**I’d build Air Spells next, then Magic Wand.** Both preserve the satisfying part of Gesture Dial: “I taught this device something, and now it recognizes me.” I’d name the workshops after the experience attendees create.

Your current 201 already provides a good teaching structure: collect examples, train locally, show predictions, and test with a partner. Here are six ways to extend that:

| Workshop idea | What attendees train and build | Main input hardware | Learning payoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Air Spells** | Teach three hand motions above a sensor—push, pull, double dip—then trigger different light and sound effects. | Modulino Distance, already used in 102/103 | Classifying movement over time; why gesture shape matters more than a single distance. |
| **Magic Wand** | Attach a motion sensor to a simple cardboard wand. Teach a swish, circle, and jab, each producing a different “spell.” | Add Modulino Movement | Multiple sensor axes, orientation, and whether a model generalizes to another person. |
| **Rhythm Lock** | Teach a personal tapping rhythm. A light-based “lock” opens when the model recognizes it, allowing some natural variation. | Add Modulino Buttons | Timing features, normalization, and the tradeoff between accepting variations and accepting the wrong rhythm. |
| **Handle With Care** | Attach a sensor to a small box. Train on gentle handling, then detect unusual shaking or abrupt movements. | Add Modulino Movement | Learning normal behavior without collecting every possible anomaly; a tangible extension of 202. |
| **Sound Scout** | Record examples of three nearby sounds—clapping, jingling keys, crumpling paper—and train a recognizer that assigns each a light pattern. | Add USB microphone | Background noise, an “unknown” class, and training data that accidentally includes misleading clues. |
| **Show & Tell** | Teach the device to recognize three objects attendees bring, then test different angles and backgrounds. | Add USB camera | Train a small classifier on pretrained image features; explore background bias and unseen examples. |

The hardware choices fit Arduino’s documented capabilities: [Distance and Buttons](https://docs.arduino.cc/libraries/arduino_modulino), [Movement’s acceleration and rotation sensing](https://docs.arduino.cc/hardware/modulino-movement/), and [UNO Q USB camera and microphone support](https://docs.arduino.cc/hardware/uno-q/). The workshop concepts above are proposals.

My priorities would be:

1. **Air Spells — easiest next addition.** Reuses hardware already in the series and could adapt 201’s capture-and-classify approach. Keep gestures toward and away from the sensor: one distance sensor cannot distinguish arbitrary left/right swipes.
2. **Magic Wand — strongest playful demo.** A different physical object gives the workshop its own identity, while keeping personal model training central.
3. **Handle With Care — strongest practical application.** Makes anomaly detection immediately understandable and gives 202’s concepts a useful physical setting.

For all of them, I’d make **“swap with a neighbor, find a failure, add examples, retrain”** part of the workshop. That is where attendees see why their training data matters.

These concepts haven’t been prototyped on UNO Q. Audio and vision need the most setup validation; Rhythm Lock should remain a recognition game, not a security mechanism.

| Workshop | What attendees do | Existing components | What they learn |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Air Spells** | Record examples of pushing, pulling, and double-dipping a hand above the sensor. Train a classifier, then cast gestures that trigger light and vibration effects. | Distance, Pixels, Vibro | Time-series classification, personal variation, and rejecting unfamiliar gestures. |
| **Rhythm Key** | Tap three personal rhythms using the **knob’s existing pushbutton**. Train the device to recognize each rhythm and display its corresponding light pattern. No rotation needed. | Knob, Pixels, Vibro | Learning timing patterns; testing whether recognition survives faster or slower tapping. |
| **Teach a Lamp** | Place a hand at different distances, turn the knob to demonstrate the brightness you want, and save examples. Train a small regression model; afterward, hand distance controls the learned brightness. | Distance, Knob, Pixels | Learning a continuous output from demonstrations, interpolation, and what happens outside the training range. |
| **Steady Hand** | Train on several comfortable hand movements toward and away from the sensor. Then challenge a partner to reproduce them without triggering an unusual-movement alert. | Distance, Pixels, Vibro | Learning a personal baseline, anomaly scores, and false alarms. |

**I’d choose Air Spells for the next workshop.** It preserves Gesture Dial’s hands-on training experience while changing the main interaction completely. The [Distance module measures range](https://docs.arduino.cc/hardware/modulino-distance/), so use motions toward and away from it; arbitrary left/right swipes aren’t distinguishable with one sensor.

**Teach a Lamp adds the most curriculum variety:** classification in 201, anomaly detection in 202, then regression through “show the device what you want.”

| **Rhythm Key** | Invent two or three tapping rhythms, record examples using the knob button, then have the device recognize them with different light and vibration responses. | A classifier using press durations and gaps. Test faster tapping, imperfect repetitions, and a partner’s attempts. |

**Rhythm Key best preserves what you like about Gesture Dial:** attendees supply labeled examples, train their own model, and immediately test whether it learned their patterns. Keep the full timing pattern so the exercise goes beyond counting taps.

**Pocket Pet provides the biggest change in character and learning method.** Training happens through feedback during play, and the finished device feels like something attendees taught.

+"""A nearest-centroid classifier for three-tap timing patterns."""
+
+import json
+import math
+from pathlib import Path
+from statistics import mean
+
+
+LABELS = ("spark", "wave", "drum")
+EXAMPLES_PER_LABEL = 5
+MINIMUM_MARGIN = 0.20
+
+
+def _vector(values):
+    if (not isinstance(values, (list, tuple)) or len(values) != 5
+            or any(type(x) not in (int, float) or not math.isfinite(x) or x <= 0 for x in values)
+            or not math.isclose(sum(values), 1.0, abs_tol=1e-6)):
+        raise ValueError("Expected five positive, normalized timing features")
+
+
+def extract_features(taps):
+    """Taps are (start_ms, end_ms), relative to the beginning of this rhythm."""
+    if len(taps) != 3:
+        raise ValueError("Use exactly three taps, then leave a one-second gap")
+    if any(len(tap) != 2 or any(type(x) is not int for x in tap) for tap in taps):
+        raise ValueError("Tap timestamps must be integer milliseconds")
+    durations = [end - start for start, end in taps]
+    gaps = [right[0] - left[1] for left, right in zip(taps, taps[1:])]
+    if any(not 80 <= value <= 1200 for value in durations):
+        raise ValueError("Hold each tap for 0.08–1.2 seconds")
+    if any(not 80 <= value < 1000 for value in gaps):
+        raise ValueError("Leave 0.08–1.0 seconds between taps")
+    timings = durations + gaps
+    return [value / sum(timings) for value in timings]
+
+
+def _distance(left, right):
+    return math.sqrt(mean((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(left, right)))
+
+
+def train(examples):
+    centroids, radii = {}, {}
+    for label in LABELS:
+        rows = examples.get(label, [])
+        if len(rows) < EXAMPLES_PER_LABEL:
+            raise ValueError(f"Record five examples of {label}")
+        for row in rows:
+            _vector(row)
+        center = [mean(column) for column in zip(*rows)]
+        centroids[label] = center
+        radii[label] = max(0.035, max(_distance(row, center) for row in rows))
+    return {"version": 1, "centroids": centroids, "radii": radii}
+
+
+def predict(model, features):
+    _vector(features)
+    distances = {label: _distance(features, model["centroids"][label]) for label in LABELS}
+    ranked = sorted(distances, key=distances.get)
+    label = ranked[0]
+    best, second = distances[label], distances[ranked[1]]
+    margin = (second - best) / max(second, 1e-9)
+    return {
+        "label": label, "margin": margin, "distances": distances,
+        "accepted": margin >= MINIMUM_MARGIN and best <= 2 * model["radii"][label],
+    }
+
+
+def save(model, path):
+    path = Path(path)
+    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
+    temporary = path.with_suffix(".tmp")
+    temporary.write_text(json.dumps(model, indent=2, allow_nan=False), encoding="utf-8")
+    temporary.replace(path)
+
+
+def load(path):
+    path = Path(path)
+    if not path.exists():
+        return None
+    model = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
+    if not isinstance(model, dict) or model.get("version") != 1:
+        raise ValueError("Unsupported rhythm model")
+    for key in ("centroids", "radii"):
+        if not isinstance(model.get(key), dict) or set(model[key]) != set(LABELS):
+            raise ValueError("Saved model must contain all three rhythms")
+    for label in LABELS:

+        radius = model["radii"][label]
+        if type(radius) not in (int, float) or not math.isfinite(radius) or not 0 < radius <= 1:

+    return model

+"""An epsilon-greedy bandit that learns which expressions get rewarded."""

+import json
+from pathlib import Path
+import random
+
+
+BEHAVIORS = ("glow", "bounce", "purr")
+EXPLORATION = 0.20

+    return {"version": 1, "counts": [0, 0, 0], "rewards": [0, 0, 0]}

+def values(model):
+    return [reward / count if count else 0.0 for reward, count in zip(model["rewards"], model["counts"])]
+
+
+def choose(model, rng=random):
+    for action, count in enumerate(model["counts"]):
+        if count == 0:
+            return action, "first example"
+    if rng.random() < EXPLORATION:
+        return rng.randrange(len(BEHAVIORS)), "explore"

+"""Separate personal reaction-time baselines for light and vibration cues."""
+
+import json
+import math
+from pathlib import Path
+from statistics import mean, pstdev
+
+
+CUES = ("light", "vibration")
+EXAMPLES_PER_CUE = 5
+MINIMUM_MS = 100
+MAXIMUM_MS = 2000
+MINIMUM_SCALE_MS = 40
+
+
+def _reaction(value):
+    if type(value) not in (int, float) or not math.isfinite(value) or not MINIMUM_MS <= value <= MAXIMUM_MS:
+        raise ValueError("Use a reaction between 100 and 2000 milliseconds")
+
+
+def train(examples):
+    baselines = {}
+    for cue in CUES:
+        rows = examples.get(cue, [])
+        if len(rows) < EXAMPLES_PER_CUE:
+            raise ValueError(f"Record five valid {cue} reactions")
+        for row in rows:
+            _reaction(row)
+        baselines[cue] = {"mean": mean(rows), "scale": max(MINIMUM_SCALE_MS, pstdev(rows))}
+    return {"version": 1, "baselines": baselines}
+
+

+    _reaction(reaction_ms)
+    if cue not in CUES:
+        raise ValueError("Unknown cue")

+    path = Path(path)
+    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

+UNO Q Qwiic -> Modulino Knob -> Modulino Pixels -> Modulino Vibro

+The order is not important for I2C, but using the same order makes debugging easier.
+
+After connecting all Modulinos, connect the UNO Q to your computer with USB-C. Rest a finger on the Vibro so you can feel its cue, keep the Pixels visible, and use your other hand for the knob button. Keep this arrangement consistent between training and testing. Release the button before starting the app.
+
+## App Lab Setup
+
+1. Open Arduino App Lab.
+2. Select your UNO Q board.
+3. If the `Updates` modal appears, **DO NOT** update the board firmware during the workshop.
+4. Open **My Apps**.
+5. Import `workshop-app.zip` from this directory.
+6. Open the imported `UNO Q Reflex Lab` app.
+7. Confirm these files are present:
+   - `app.yaml`
+   - `python/main.py`
+   - `python/button.py`
+   - `python/reflex_model.py`
+   - `sketch/sketch.ino`
+   - `sketch/sketch.yaml`
+8. Click `Run` in the top-right corner.
+9. Keep the App Lab output panel visible. It tells you which cue to expect and reports accepted, false-start, and timeout results.
+
+App Lab compiles and flashes the MCU sketch, then starts the Python runtime on the UNO Q Linux side. The Vibro pulses once during startup; this is not a trial cue. No additional Python packages or model downloads are required beyond the App Lab runtime.
+
+## Train Your Reaction Baseline
+
+The first run collects five valid responses to each cue in this order:
+
+1. `light`: press when all eight Pixels turn white.
+2. `vibration`: press when you feel the short Vibro pulse. The single amber waiting Pixel stays unchanged during this cue.
+
+For every example:
+
+1. Read the requested cue in the output.
+2. Tap and release the knob to arm the trial. This start tap lasts 0.08–0.6 seconds and is not a measured reaction.
+3. When one amber Pixel is lit, wait without pressing. The cue arrives after a random delay of 1.5–3.5 seconds.
+4. Press as soon as you notice the cue, then release. The measured response ends on the press, not the release.
+5. Read the response time and wait for the next ready prompt before starting another round.
+
+Pressing before the cue is a false start. Responses under 100 ms are rejected as anticipations; no response within two seconds is a timeout. Rejected trials do not advance training or change the model. Keep responding naturally rather than deliberately slowing down to alter the baseline.
+
+| Color or pattern | Meaning |
+| --- | --- |
+| Pink Pixels | Collecting light reactions |
+| Purple Pixels | Collecting vibration reactions |
+| One amber Pixel | Armed and waiting; do not press yet |
+| Eight white Pixels | Light cue: press now |
+| One amber Pixel plus a 120 ms vibration | Vibration cue: press now |
+| Eight green Pixels during training | Valid example accepted |
+| Three amber Pixels after a trial | False start, anticipation, or timeout; read the output |
+| Blue Pixels | Trained baseline ready for a challenge |
+| Red Pixels | Saved baseline could not be erased; check the output |
+
+The number of training Pixels shows progress for the current cue, with at least one Pixel lit. The output gives the exact example number. Results remain visible for at least one second and until the button is released.
+
+## Use The Trained Reflex Lab
+
+After the tenth valid reaction, the Linux application trains and saves the two baselines. Tap and release to start each new challenge. The app randomly selects a light or vibration cue and names it in the output before the waiting period.
+
+- Green indicates a response within two learned scales of your mean: `typical`.
+- Purple indicates a response more than two scales below your mean: `faster`.
+- Amber indicates a response more than two scales above your mean: `slower`.
+- More lit Pixels indicate a larger absolute deviation, reaching eight at four scales.
+
+Watch the output for the cue, reaction time in milliseconds, category, and signed deviation. Negative scores mean faster than the baseline; positive scores mean slower. The score is not a probability or a population ranking. Errors and slower responses both use amber, so read the output to distinguish them.
+
+Challenge rounds do not update the saved baseline. Hold the knob down for three seconds at any time to erase it and retrain. Release before starting a new round. An active trial is cancelled when the reset is detected.
+
+## How The Demo Works
+
+```mermaid
+flowchart LR
+    K["Tap and release to arm"] --> P["Linux: select cue and random delay"]
+    P -->|"Bridge RPC"| W["MCU: wait, then present cue"]
+    W --> T["MCU: timestamp button response"]
+    T --> G{"Valid reaction?"}
+    G -->|"No"| R["Retry without learning"]
+    G -->|"Yes"| M["Linux: train or score cue baseline"]
+    M -->|"Bridge RPC"| O["Pixels show result"]
+```
+
+### MCU Responsibilities
+
+- Sample the pushbutton at a target interval of 5 ms and debounce changes for 20 ms.
+- Run the waiting period, issue the cue, and time the response on the same MCU clock.
+- Timestamp an accepted press at the beginning of its stable transition.
+- Detect false starts and timeouts even while Linux is waiting on a Bridge call.
+- Keep vibration trials free of a simultaneous visual cue.
+- Buffer button events for the app's start and reset controls and expose safe Bridge callbacks.
+
+### Linux MPU Responsibilities
+
+- Choose the cue and random waiting duration, then request a trial.
+- Collect five valid responses per cue and exclude retries from training.
+- Learn separate means and variation scales for light and vibration.
+- Score challenge rounds against the fixed baseline.
+- Save the model to `data/reflex_model.json` using an atomic file replacement.
+
+## The Model
+
+This workshop uses a statistical model implemented with the Python standard library. For each cue, training calculates the mean reaction time and population standard deviation. A minimum scale of 40 ms prevents nearly identical training examples from making the model oversensitive.
+
+```text
+scale = max(training standard deviation, 40 milliseconds)
+signed deviation = (new reaction time - training mean) / scale
+```
+
+A score below `-2` is faster, above `2` is slower, and between those bounds, including the boundaries, is typical. This is a comparison with one participant's examples, not a claim about whether a reaction is good or bad.
+
+The complete learning loop is:
+
+```text
+present cue -> collect valid response -> learn baseline -> score fresh trials -> retrain
+```
+
+The MCU measures from completion of the cue command to the detected button transition, so Bridge round-trip time is not included. Sensor polling, I2C calls, LED updates, and motor startup still affect physical timing. This is a workshop experiment, not a calibrated reaction-time instrument. Five examples per cue make training short but produce a rough baseline; use more examples for a more stable estimate.
+
+## Suggested Experiments
+
+- Compare the learned light and vibration means, keeping your hand positions consistent.
+- Run ten fresh challenges and count typical, faster, slower, and invalid trials separately.
+- Swap participants without retraining, then retrain and compare the results.
+- Deliberately anticipate the cue and verify that false starts do not enter the dataset.
+- Retrain after practice and compare the old and new means printed in the output.
+- Change `MINIMUM_SCALE_MS` in `reflex_model.py` and compare how often ordinary responses are flagged.
+
+## Troubleshooting
+
+### My trial reports a false start
+
+Release the start tap fully. Wait through the single amber Pixel and press only when all eight Pixels turn white or you feel the vibration cue. The result output explains which condition failed.
+
+### Vibration trials time out
+
+Keep a finger resting on the Vibro and respond with your other hand. Check that the startup pulse can be felt. The waiting Pixel intentionally does not change when the vibration cue occurs.
+
+### Ordinary responses are marked faster or slower
+
+The result is relative to your own small training set. Keep your posture and hand positions consistent, collect representative responses, and retrain. The 40 ms minimum scale is adjustable in `reflex_model.py`.
+
+### The app skips training when restarted
+
+The baseline is intentionally persistent. Hold for three seconds to erase it. If saving fails, the active baseline remains in memory, but a restart may restore an older model or require training again.
+
+### The output reports a button buffer overflow
+
+The trial is cancelled. Release the button, then tap to arm another trial. Repeated overflows or malformed packets require restarting the app and checking board communication.
